title: SEBI Moves to Let NRIs Complete Investment KYC Online From Abroad
excerpt: Chairman Tuhin Kanta Pandey confirmed SEBI will simplify digital onboarding and KYC for overseas investors; the proposal drops the requirement that an investor's phone location be inside India.
body:
• SEBI chairman Tuhin Kanta Pandey said on October 24 that the regulator will make it easier for overseas investors, including NRIs, to invest in India through digital onboarding, simplified KYC and reduced paperwork, while keeping regulatory safeguards.
  • The underlying proposal would drop the rule that an investor's phone location must be inside India during digital KYC — today that single rule forces most NRIs abroad to courier signed, certified documents or wait for a trip home.
  • The consultation drew more than 400 comments, and SEBI has said a circular will be issued shortly.
  • For NRIs in FATF-compliant countries such as the US, the proposal means completing KYC from home: submit documents through an app or website, sign electronically, and verify over video.

India's market regulator is moving to let non-resident Indians open and verify investment accounts without setting foot in India. SEBI chairman Tuhin Kanta Pandey told an industry convention on October 24 that the Securities and Exchange Board of India would make it easier for overseas investors, including NRIs, to invest in India through digital onboarding, simplified know-your-customer processes and reduced paperwork, while maintaining regulatory safeguards, according to IANS reporting carried by NewKerala.

The one rule that blocks NRIs today

"If the circular lands as proposed, an NRI in a FATF-compliant country will be able to complete the entire KYC from home, and carry that verified record from one intermediary to the next."

The barrier is technical. Under the current framework, digital KYC captures the investor's location through latitude and longitude, and that location must be within India. An NRI sitting in New Jersey or Toronto therefore cannot complete digital onboarding at all: the standard route is a physical application, or signed and certified documents sent to the intermediary by courier, with the cost and delay that involves.

SEBI's consultation paper, published on August 14, proposes removing that restriction for individual Persons Resident Outside India (PROIs) — NRIs, Overseas Citizens of India and eligible foreign nationals — who are located in countries compliant with the standards of the Financial Action Task Force (FATF), the global anti-money-laundering watchdog. The United States, Canada, the United Kingdom and most major diaspora destinations are FATF members or in FATF-style regional bodies, so the large majority of NRIs would fall inside the relaxed regime. Existing requirements would continue for clients in FATF non-compliant countries.

How digital onboarding would work

Under the proposed framework described by Cafemutual and analysed by KPMG in India, an overseas investor would submit the KYC form and supporting documents through an app, website or another digital channel. Documents could be authenticated with an electronic or digital signature, including Aadhaar e-sign where available. Investors could submit a cropped image of their specimen signature, but would give a wet signature during Video In-Person Verification (VIPV), which the intermediary matches against the submitted signature.

The proposal also takes aim at two long-standing irritants: dependence on an Indian mobile number for OTP authentication, and having to repeat the full KYC with every new intermediary. SEBI has proposed making KYC records portable across securities-market intermediaries — described in its press material as "one KYC for multiple intermediaries" — so an investor already verified with one broker or fund house could reuse that record, with additional checks left to each intermediary's risk assessment.

Where the process stands

This is a proposal, not yet a live facility. Pandey said earlier this month that SEBI had received more than 400 comments on the consultation and would issue a circular shortly. The October 24 remarks, made alongside announcements on graded broker compliance and an AI sandbox, signal that the NRI onboarding change remains an active priority rather than a shelved consultation.

For the diaspora, the stakes are concrete. NRI investment in Indian mutual funds and equities has grown steadily, but onboarding friction — couriers, notarised copies, KYCs that can only be finished during a trip to India — is the most common reason accounts stall before the first investment. If the circular lands as proposed, an NRI in a FATF-compliant country will be able to complete the entire KYC from home, and carry that verified record from one intermediary to the next.
